source.author: José Raúl Capablanca
source.section: Chapter I, §4 Some Winning Positions in the Middle-game, Example 14

narration.say: The same type of combination, in a more complicated form.
The knight wants to go to f6, but the black knight on d7 guards that square.

steps.title: Your turn: remove the guard
steps.source: 1. B x Kt, Q x B. If …B x Kt; Q - B 3 threatens mate, and therefore wins the Q, which is already attacked.

narration.say: Your move. Get rid of the defender of f6.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Remove the knight that guards f6.

feedback.*: The bishop on b5 can take the knight on d7.

exercise.success: 1. Bxd7. Black takes back with the queen.

narration.say: If Black had taken the knight on e4 instead, queen to c3 would threaten mate on g7.
And the black queen was already attacked, so Black would lose it.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Give the knight check.

narration.say: This time it is the rook that uses the open g-file.

exercise.prompt: White to move. Check along the g-file.

feedback.*: The rook swings to the g-file with check.

exercise.success: 3. Rg3, check. Black goes to h8.

exercise.prompt: White to move and give checkmate in one.

feedback.*: The bishop on b2 takes with check.

narration.say: When a key square is guarded, first remove the guard.
Recognising a pattern lets you find combinations in more complicated positions.
